There isn’t some giant government bank that guarantees the value of your brokerage account.

The first protection is much simpler: your stocks and ETFs are customer assets. They’re generally supposed to be kept separate from the brokerage firm’s own assets, so if the brokerage goes bankrupt, its creditors don’t simply get to take your shares.

SIPC is the additional backstop if an SIPC-member brokerage fails and customer assets are actually missing. Btw, SIPC isn’t a government agency; it’s a nonprofit membership corporation created under federal law. It does not protect you against market losses. So if the stock market falls 50%, your portfolio can absolutely fall 50%. Nobody reimburses you for that.

Lehman actually illustrates the distinction pretty well. Lehman shareholders and creditors suffered enormous losses, but roughly 110,000 brokerage customer accounts containing about $92 billion were transferred to solvent firms and received 100% recoveries through those transfers.

The protection is about ownership and custody of the securities, not protection from a falling market.

text:
@jeffferguson4632 Good point. Legally, SVB did not eliminate the $250,000 FDIC limit. Regulators used the “systemic risk exception,” which is extraordinary authority that allowed them to protect uninsured depositors because they believed losses could trigger broader bank runs. The statutory insurance limit itself never changed. 

So depositors above $250,000 at the next failed bank would not automatically have a legal right to the same treatment. Another systemic-risk determination would have to be made.

But, I do think SVB created an expectation problem. If uninsured depositors at one large bank are made whole because regulators fear contagion, depositors at the next large bank may reasonably expect the same, and depositors at a smaller bank could understandably ask why they were treated differently. In fact, that moral-hazard/fairness issue was one of the concerns raised after SVB.

So I wouldn’t call the $250,000 limit “gone,” but SVB definitely blurred the line between what is formally insured and what the government might choose to protect in a systemic crisis.
